name: Poisson Stippling
basis: hist: 'stippling is an old technique in pen and ink illustration'; how: dots never closer than a radius that shrinks in the shadows
note: Framed as blue-noise sampling; filed as pen stippling because the output follows the stippler's rule. Dots are perfect discs.

lumenary.blurb: Dots placed no closer than a set distance, the distance shrinking in the shadows. The result is even in texture and dense where it is dark.

why: Random dots clump and leave gaps, while a grid shows its rows. The eye prefers something in between: dots that are random but never too close. This is called blue noise, and it looks smooth and natural because it has no long-range pattern. Here the minimum distance shrinks in the shadows, so the dots crowd together there and thin out in the lights.
how: Set the minimum distance r(x) = r_max − (r_max − r_min) h^γ, where h is the darkness under the point and γ the contrast.
Try random points, up to 4.5 times the area divided by r_min², at most 900,000 of them.
Keep a point only if its distance from every dot kept so far is at least the mean of the two radii.
Use a grid of cells r_max wide so only the nine nearest cells need checking.
Draw each dot in ink, sepia or the picture’s colour.
history: Stippling is an old technique in pen and ink illustration, used for botany and anatomy. Robert Cook introduced stochastic sampling to computer graphics in 1986, and Don Mitchell and others developed blue noise sampling in the early 1990s. Robert Bridson published a fast algorithm in 2007. The psychologist John Yellott observed in 1983 that the receptor cells in a monkey’s eye are arranged in a similar pattern.
uses: Pen and ink style illustration and print
Sampling for ray tracing and image processing
Placing trees, rocks and stars in games
terms: Random points with no clumps and no regular pattern.
Random sampling in which no two points are closer than a chosen distance.
To make tone by a pattern of dots.
paragraphs: Stippling makes tone from dots. Placing them at random leaves clumps and gaps that look wrong, whereas placing them on a grid shows the grid. Poisson-disk sampling is in between: dots are random, but no two are closer than a minimum distance. Here the minimum distance is not fixed but follows the picture: r(x) = r_max − (r_max − r_min) h^γ, where h is the heaviness (darkness on light paper) and γ the contrast slider. Random points are tried (up to 4.5 times the area divided by r_min², at most 900,000), and a point is kept if its distance to every dot already kept is at least the mean of the two radii, (r_p + r_q)/2. A grid of cells r_max wide means only the nine nearest cells are searched.

The result is blue noise: even in texture, with no long-range pattern. Because each dot excludes a disc of about r around it, the number of dots per unit area goes roughly as 1/r², so the density rises quickly as the spacing shrinks, and the shadows are dark. The dots are also larger in the shadows, by up to 1.95 times (1 + 0.95 h²), and their colour is black, sepia, cream on night paper or the picture’s own, darkened.

equations.note: The local minimum spacing; h is the heaviness of the picture at x.

equations.tex: \text{keep }\mathbf p\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \lVert\mathbf p-\mathbf q\rVert\ \ge\ \tfrac12\big(r(\mathbf p)+r(\mathbf q)\big)\quad\text{for every kept }\mathbf q
